body:
Godot's import system is designed to rewrite files, as it will often add things like mipmaps or other metadata the source image does not have. It can also perform operations that modify the image data, such as resizing it, remapping color/alpha channels and so on.

To make lossy WebPs reused as-is, we would need to ensure there are *no* import options that change the visuals in use. You would still need to encode mipmaps as well (if mipmaps are enabled), so there would still be some amount of time spent on WebP encoding. Doing this would already add a significant amount of complexity on its own, not to mention a higher chance for bugs to pop up in the future. Therefore, I'm not sure it's worth the effort.

I would recommend you use lossless WebP source files whenever possible, as they are more efficient than PNG while still being lossless (which means they won't suffer from [generation loss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_loss) as you iterate on them). File sizes might seem high at a glance, but a 2D or stylized project has much more leeway than a realistic 3D project here (most realistic 3D game project repositories eventually cross the 100 GB mark, while this is much less common with 2D).

In any case, the size of source files has no bearing on the exported project, as this is determined by import settings instead.

> When a lossless WebP is imported with "Lossless" compression, it is still re-encoded. This is a redundant computation that wastes significant time during import, when a simple file copy would achieve the identical result instantly.

Re-encoding a lossless WebP isn't always a waste of time, as lossless WebP still has different compression efficiency levels (it's a tradeoff between encoding speed and compression ratio). If the source lossless WebP uses a preset that favors speed, we can use a preset that favors compression ratio instead.
